items.pronunciation_notes: Unaspirated क with no puff of air — the k of English 'skate', not 'kite'. One syllable, kaan.

learn.explanation_en: कान is an ear. Like most body parts that come in pairs you will hear it in the plural as often as the singular, and the plural is unchanged. It ends in a consonant and is masculine, which the ending does not tell you. Keep the first sound free of breath: खान, with a puff of air, means a mine.

examples.note: The plural is identical to the singular.
बड़े takes -े for a masculine plural.
In the singular the adjective takes -ा instead.

practice.question: कान
practice.explanation_en: कान is an ear. नाक is a nose and आँख an eye.

game.question_en: राम ___ कान — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: कान is masculine, so का. Its consonant ending gives no clue at all.

items.pronunciation_notes: Dental न with the tongue on the teeth, and an unaspirated क at the end: naak.

learn.explanation_en: नाक is the nose, and it is feminine. That is worth pausing on, because it sits right beside कान and हाथ, which look structurally identical — three body parts, three consonant endings, and नाक is the odd one out. There is no pattern to lean on here. The gender is a property of the word and has to be memorised with it.

examples.note: लंबी takes -ी because नाक is feminine.
Compare बड़े कान, where the same adjective takes -े.
One feminine, one masculine, both ending in consonants.

common_error.why_en: नाक is feminine, so the adjective takes -ी — unlike कान, which takes -ा.

practice.question: नाक
practice.explanation_en: नाक is the nose. कान is an ear and मुँह a mouth.

game.question_en: राम ___ नाक — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: नाक is feminine, so की — while कान, which also ends in a consonant, takes का.

items.pronunciation_notes: The inherent vowel on ह drops, so the word is said in two syllables as chehraa rather than chehaaraa.

learn.explanation_en: चेहरा is the face. It ends in -ा and is masculine, so the ending predicts correctly and the plural changes to चेहरे in the ordinary way. The word doubles as a small schwa exercise: written out it looks like three syllables, but the inherent vowel on ह disappears, leaving two.

examples.note: गोल never changes form, whatever the noun.
The -ा becomes -े in the plural.
साफ़ carries the dotted letter from Module 2.

practice.question: चेहरा
practice.explanation_en: चेहरा is the face as a whole. सिर is the head and मुँह the mouth.

game.question_en: राम ___ चेहरा — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: चेहरा is masculine, so का. The -ा ending predicts correctly.

summary.recap_en: This level added कान, नाक and चेहरा. नाक is the one to remember: it looks exactly like कान and हाथ but is feminine, which is why consonant endings are treated as giving no information.
summary.next_up_en: Next: पैर, उँगली and पेट, including one word whose ending finally predicts correctly.

items.pronunciation_notes: The ऐ is a single open vowel close to the a of 'cat' — the word rhymes roughly with 'pear', not with 'pyre'.

learn.explanation_en: पैर covers both the foot and, in ordinary speech, the leg as well — Hindi does not insist on the distinction English makes. It is masculine and ends in a consonant, so the gender is unpredictable. Do not let the transliteration mislead you: the vowel is the open ऐ from Module 1, so this is said with the vowel of 'pet', not the sound of English 'pyre'.

examples.note: The plural is unchanged.
बड़े takes -े for a masculine plural.
The usual way to say barefoot.

practice.question: पैर
practice.explanation_en: पैर is a foot, and in everyday speech the leg as well. हाथ is a hand.

game.question_en: राम ___ पैर — का, के or की?

items.pronunciation_notes: The crescent nasalises the opening vowel and the inherent vowel on ग drops, giving ũglii in two syllables.

learn.explanation_en: उँगली is a finger, and it covers toes as well, with पैर की उँगली meaning a toe. It ends in -ी and is feminine, so the ending predicts correctly, and the plural follows the -ियाँ pattern you saw in बेटियाँ. Two things happen when you say it: the crescent nasalises the first vowel, and the inherent vowel on ग drops out entirely.

examples.note: छोटी takes -ी to match the feminine noun.
The -ी becomes -ियाँ in the plural.
Feminine adjectives keep -ी in the plural too.

common_error.why_en: The long ी shortens to ि before the plural ending, exactly as it does in बेटियाँ.

practice.question: उँगली
practice.explanation_en: उँगली is a finger. हाथ is the hand it belongs to.

game.question_en: राम ___ उँगली — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: उँगली is feminine, so की. The -ी ending predicts correctly here.

items.pronunciation_notes: Retroflex ट with the tongue curled back, and a flat ए with no glide after it: peṭ.

learn.explanation_en: पेट is the stomach or belly, and it is the word used for hunger and for stomach trouble alike. It is masculine and ends in a consonant, so the gender is unpredictable. The final letter is the retroflex ट, so curl the tongue back rather than letting it land where an English t would.

examples.note: The masculine adjective ending.
खाली ends in -ी but never changes form.
भरा takes -ा to agree.

practice.question: पेट
practice.explanation_en: पेट is the stomach. पीठ is the back.

game.question_en: राम ___ पेट — का, के or की?

summary.recap_en: This level covered पैर, उँगली and पेट. उँगली is the only one whose ending predicts its gender, and it also packs in a nasalised vowel and a dropped medial schwa.
summary.next_up_en: Next: दाँत, पीठ and बाल complete the body words, including one noun that is normally plural.

items.pronunciation_notes: The crescent nasalises the vowel, and both consonants are dental — the tongue stays on the teeth from start to finish: dãat.

learn.explanation_en: दाँत is a tooth, and like कान and पैर it does not change in the plural, which is convenient since teeth are usually talked about several at a time. It is masculine with a consonant ending, so the gender is unpredictable. The word is also a compact pronunciation test: the crescent nasalises the vowel, and both द and त are dental, so the tongue never leaves the teeth.

examples.note: सफ़ेद never changes form.
टूटा takes -ा to agree with the masculine noun.
The plural is identical to the singular.

practice.question: दाँत
practice.explanation_en: दाँत is a tooth. मुँह is the mouth it sits in.

game.question_en: राम ___ दाँत — का, के or की?

items.pronunciation_notes: The final ठ is a retroflex released with breath — the tongue curls back and a puff follows: piiṭh.

learn.explanation_en: पीठ is the back. It is feminine, joining नाक and आँख as consonant-ending body parts that turn out not to be masculine — three out of the eight covered here, which is often enough that guessing masculine is a poor strategy. The final letter is the aspirated retroflex ठ, so the tongue curls back and breath is released after it.

examples.note: सीधी takes -ी because पीठ is feminine.
चौड़ी contains the flap ड़ from Module 2.
One feminine, one masculine, both ending in consonants.

common_error.why_en: पीठ is feminine, so the adjective takes -ी — while पेट, also a consonant ending, takes -ा.

practice.question: पीठ
practice.explanation_en: पीठ is the back. पेट is the stomach on the other side.

game.question_en: राम ___ पीठ — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: पीठ is feminine, so की. Its consonant ending predicts nothing.

items.pronunciation_notes: The crescent nasalises the vowel and the final ह is light, giving one syllable: mũh.

learn.explanation_en: मुँह is the mouth. It is masculine and ends in a consonant, so the gender is unpredictable and has to be learned. The crescent nasalises the vowel, so nothing like an n is pronounced, and the final ह is light enough that the whole word is a single syllable. It is also used more widely than the English word, covering the face in some fixed phrases.

examples.note: बड़ा takes -ा because मुँह is masculine.
खुला also takes -ा to agree.
One masculine, one feminine, both ending in consonants.

practice.question: मुँह
practice.explanation_en: मुँह is the mouth. दाँत are the teeth inside it and नाक is the nose.

game.question_en: राम ___ मुँह — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: मुँह is masculine, so का. Its consonant ending gives no clue.

summary.recap_en: This level finished the body words with दाँत, पीठ and मुँह. Of the twelve body words, four turned out to be feminine and eight masculine, with no ending reliably predicting which.
summary.next_up_en: Next: food and drink, opening with the two most useful nouns in the language and the gender trap in each.

items.pronunciation_notes: A long aa then a long ii, with a dental न between them: paanii.

learn.explanation_en: पानी is water, and it is the single most important gender exception in the language for a learner to get right, simply because you will say it several times a day. It ends in -ी, which normally marks a feminine noun, and it is masculine. It belongs with भाई and आदमी in that small group of misleading -ी words. Being a mass noun it has no real plural, and the form never changes.

examples.note: ठंडा takes -ा because पानी is masculine.
गरम never changes form, so it hides the gender.
Another adjective that stays the same whatever the noun.

common_error.why_en: पानी ends in -ी but is masculine, so the adjective takes -ा. This is one of the most frequent mistakes learners make.

practice.question: पानी
practice.explanation_en: पानी is water. दूध is milk and चाय is tea.

game.question_en: राम ___ पानी — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: पानी is masculine, so का — despite the -ी ending, which is exactly why this word is flagged.

items.pronunciation_notes: Light unaspirated च — the ch of English 'church' but with no puff of air. One syllable, chaay.

learn.explanation_en: चाय is tea, and you will be offered it more often than any other noun in this module will come up. It is feminine, and since it ends in a consonant the ending gives you nothing to work from. Set it beside पानी on the last card: two everyday drinks, two opposite genders, and neither ending pointing the right way. Both have to be learned outright.

examples.note: गरम is one of the adjectives that never changes.
अच्छी takes -ी because चाय is feminine.
मीठी also takes -ी to agree.

common_error.why_en: चाय is feminine, so the adjective takes -ी.

practice.question: चाय
practice.explanation_en: चाय is tea. पानी is water and दूध is milk.

game.question_en: राम ___ चाय — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: चाय is feminine, so की — while पानी, from the same category, takes का.

items.pronunciation_notes: Retroflex ट with the tongue curled back, and a flat ओ with no w-glide: roṭii.

learn.explanation_en: रोटी is the flatbread eaten with almost every meal in north India. It ends in -ी and is feminine, so the ending predicts correctly for once, and the plural follows the -ियाँ pattern. Put it next to पानी from two cards back and the point of this whole module becomes visible: identical endings, opposite genders, and only the word itself tells you which.

examples.note: An adjective that does not change form.
The -ी becomes -ियाँ in the plural.
ताज़ी carries the dotted ज़ and takes -ी to agree.

practice.question: रोटी
practice.explanation_en: रोटी is flatbread. चावल is rice and दाल is lentils.

game.question_en: राम ___ रोटी — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: रोटी is feminine, so की. The -ी ending predicts correctly here, unlike in पानी.

summary.recap_en: This level opened food and drink with पानी, चाय and रोटी. पानी and रोटी share an ending and take opposite genders, which makes them the clearest pair in the module for showing that endings cannot be trusted.
summary.next_up_en: Next: दूध, खाना and दाल, including a word that is also a verb and a word that changes meaning if your tongue slips.

items.pronunciation_notes: A plain dental द at the front and a breathy dental ध at the end, with a long vowel between: duudh.

learn.explanation_en: दूध is milk. It ends in a consonant and is masculine, so the gender has to be learned. The word is also a compact pronunciation exercise you have met before: both consonants are dental, so the tongue stays on the teeth, and the second one is released with breath while the first is not.

examples.note: ठंडा takes -ा because दूध is masculine.
An adjective that never changes form.
ताज़ा here, but ताज़ी with रोटी — the ending follows the noun.

practice.question: दूध
practice.explanation_en: दूध is milk. दही is curd, and it is masculine too despite ending in -ी.

game.question_en: राम ___ दूध — का, के or की?

items.pronunciation_notes: Aspirated ख with a clear puff of breath, then two long vowels: khaanaa.

learn.explanation_en: खाना is food. It is masculine and ends in -ा, so both its gender and its plural behave predictably. It also has a second life worth knowing about now, even though the grammar arrives much later: the same word is the verb 'to eat'. Hindi names its verbs this way, so खाना is both the meal and the act of eating it, and only the surrounding sentence tells you which is meant.

examples.note: The masculine adjective ending.
An adjective that does not change.
का takes its masculine form because खाना, the word after it, is masculine.

practice.question: खाना
practice.explanation_en: खाना is food. The same word is also the verb 'to eat', which arrives in Module 7.

game.question_en: राम ___ खाना — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: खाना is masculine, so का. The -ा ending predicts correctly.

items.pronunciation_notes: Dental द with the tongue on the teeth. Curl the tongue back instead and you get डाल, which means a branch.

learn.explanation_en: दाल is lentils, and the dish made from them that appears at most meals. This is the word Module 1 used to introduce the dental and retroflex split, so it carries two lessons at once: the tongue must press against the teeth rather than curl back, and the word is feminine despite a consonant ending that tells you nothing. Order it with the tongue in the wrong place and you have asked for a tree branch.

examples.note: An adjective that does not change form.
अच्छी takes -ी because दाल is feminine.
Two feminine nouns, and the most everyday meal there is.

common_error.why_en: दाल is feminine, so the adjective takes -ी — while दूध, also a consonant ending, takes -ा.

practice.question: दाल
practice.explanation_en: दाल is lentils. डाल, said with the tongue curled back, is a branch — the pair from Module 1.

game.question_en: राम ___ दाल — का, के or की?

summary.recap_en: This level covered दूध, खाना and दाल. दूध and दाल both end in consonants and take opposite genders, and दाल is also the word that tests whether your tongue is on the teeth or curled back.
summary.next_up_en: Next: more food and drink, including rice, vegetables and the words for sweet and salty.
